evidence: Directly stated with heritability estimates.

claim: A matrix spectral decomposition analysis estimated the effective number of independent facial traits as 43.

claim: The study-wide significant threshold was set at 1.2 × 10−9.
source: A matrix spectral decomposition analysis estimated the effective number of independent facial traits as 43, which corresponds to a Bonferroni corrected study-wide significant threshold of 1.2 × 10−9.

claim: In the discovery GWAS meta-analysis, a total of 221 SNPs from six distinct loci showed study-wide significant association (p<1.2 × 10−9) with facial phenotypes.
source: In the discovery GWAS meta-analysis, a total of 221 SNPs from six distinct loci showed study-wide significant association (p<1.2 × 10−9) with facial phenotypes, among which two have not been previously reported: 4q28.1 INTU (top SNP rs1250495 p=3.03 × 10−10), and 12q24.21 TBX3 (rs1863716 p=1.47 × 10−10).
evidence: Directly stated with specific numbers and p-values.

claim: Two novel face-associated loci were identified: 4q28.1 INTU (top SNP rs1250495 p=3.03 × 10−10), and 12q24.21 TBX3 (rs1863716 p=1.47 × 10−10).
source: In the discovery GWAS meta-analysis, a total of 221 SNPs from six distinct loci showed study-wide significant association (p<1.2 × 10−9) with facial phenotypes, among which two have not been previously reported: 4q28.1 INTU (top SNP rs1250495 p=3.03 × 10−10), and 12q24.21 TBX3 (rs1863716 p=1.47 × 10−10).

source: The other four have been described in previous GWASs of facial variation, including 2q36.1 PAX3, 4q31.3 SFRP2, 17q24.3 CASC17, and 20p11.22 PAX1 (Figure 1 and Supplementary file 1 - Table 7) (Liu et al., 2012; Paternoster et al., 2012; Adhikari et al., 2016; Shaffer et al., 2016; Claes et al., 2018).
evidence: Directly stated with citations to previous studies.

claim: 273 SNPs from 18 distinct loci passed the 5 × 10−8 threshold in addition to the study-wide significant ones.
source: In addition to the study-wide significant ones, 273 SNPs from 18 distinct loci passed the 5 × 10−8 threshold (Supplementary file 1 - Table 7), of which 15 were novel and 3 (1p12 TBX15, 9q22.31 ROR2 and 17q24.3 SOX9) have been reported in previous studies (Cha et al., 2018; Claes et al., 2018; Pickrell et al., 2016).
evidence: Directly stated with specific numbers and citations.

claim: 15 novel loci were identified at the suggestive significance threshold.

evidence: Directly stated as novel findings.

claim: In total, 24 face-associated genetic loci were identified, of which 17 were not reported in previous face GWASs.
source: Thus, in total, we identified 24 face-associated genetic loci, of which 17 were not reported in previous face GWASs, that we followed-up via a multi-ethnic replication analysis (see below).
evidence: Directly stated as a summary of findings.

claim: Only one SNP (rs3403289 at 2q36.1 PAX3) showed nominally significant heterogeneity between the discovery cohorts.
source: In general, no significant heterogeneity was observed for the 24 top SNPs of the study-wide significant and suggestive associated loci, that is only one SNP (rs3403289 at 2q36.1 PAX3) showed nominally significant (Cochran's Q test p=0.04, Table 1) heterogeneity between the discovery cohorts, but was not significant after multiple testing correction.
evidence: Directly stated with statistical test result.

claim: After Bonferroni correction of multiple testing of 24 SNPs, significant evidence of replication (p<2.1×10−3) was obtained for 10 SNPs.
source: After Bonferroni correction of multiple testing of 24 SNPs, significant evidence of replication (p<2.1×10−3) was obtained for 10 SNPs, among which six were novel loci: 1p36.22 CASZ1, 4q28.1 INTU, 6p21.2 KIF6, 12q24.21 TBX3, 14q32.2 C14orf64, and 16q12.2 RPGRIP1L (Figure 2), and four have been described in previous face GWASs: 2q36.1 PAX3, 4q31.3 SFRP2, 9q22.31 ROR2, and 20p11.22 PAX1 (Adhikari et al., 2016; Claes et al., 2018; Paternoster et al., 2012; Pickrell et al., 2016; Shaffer et al., 2016).
evidence: Directly stated with statistical threshold and specific loci.

claim: Six novel loci were successfully replicated: 1p36.22 CASZ1, 4q28.1 INTU, 6p21.2 KIF6, 12q24.21 TBX3, 14q32.2 C14orf64, and 16q12.2 RPGRIP1L.
source: After Bonferroni correction of multiple testing of 24 SNPs, significant evidence of replication (p<2.1×10−3) was obtained for 10 SNPs, among which six were novel loci: 1p36.22 CASZ1, 4q28.1 INTU, 6p21.2 KIF6, 12q24.21 TBX3, 14q32.2 C14orf64, and 16q12.2 RPGRIP1L (Figure 2), and four have been described in previous face GWASs: 2q36.1 PAX3, 4q31.3 SFRP2, 9q22.31 ROR2, and 20p11.22 PAX1 (Adhikari et al., 2016; Claes et al., 2018; Paternoster et al., 2012; Pickrell et al., 2016; Shaffer et al., 2016).

claim: Four previously reported loci were replicated: 2q36.1 PAX3, 4q31.3 SFRP2, 9q22.31 ROR2, and 20p11.22 PAX1.
source: After Bonferroni correction of multiple testing of 24 SNPs, significant evidence of replication (p<2.1×10−3) was obtained for 10 SNPs, among which six were novel loci: 1p36.22 CASZ1, 4q28.1 INTU, 6p21.2 KIF6, 12q24.21 TBX3, 14q32.2 C14orf64, and 16q12.2 RPGRIP1L (Figure 2), and four have been described in previous face GWASs: 2q36.1 PAX3, 4q31.3 SFRP2, 9q22.31 ROR2, and 20p11.22 PAX1 (Adhikari et al., 2016; Claes et al., 2018; Paternoster et al., 2012; Pickrell et al., 2016; Shaffer et al., 2016).

claim: The 31 SNPs individually explain less than 1%, and together explain up to 4.62%, of the variance for individual phenotypes.
source: These 31 SNPs individually explain less than 1%, and together explain up to 4.62%, of the variance for individual phenotypes (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: Directly stated with specific variance values.

claim: The polygenic face scores based on the 31 SNPs were largely reversely distributed between EUR and AFR, with EAS situated in between.
source: The polygenic face scores based on the 31 SNPs were largely reversely distributed between EUR and AFR, with EAS situated in between (Figure 3C).
evidence: Directly stated with reference to figure.

claim: EUR showed the longest distances among the vertical phenotypes, while AFR had the widest of the horizontal phenotypes.
source: EUR showed the longest distances among the vertical phenotypes, while AFR had the widest of the horizontal phenotypes.
evidence: Directly stated as observation from polygenic scores.

claim: A gene ontology enrichment analysis for the 24 face-associated genetic loci highlighted a total of 67 biological process terms and seven molecular function terms significantly enriched (FDR < 0.01 or q value < 0.01).
source: A gene ontology enrichment analysis for the 24 face-associated genetic loci (Table 1) highlighted a total of 67 biological process terms and seven molecular function terms significantly enriched with different genes group (FDR < 0.01 or q value < 0.01, Supplementary file 1 - Table 15), with the top significant terms being 'embryonic digit morphogenesis' and 'embryonic appendage morphogenesis' (FDR < 1 × 10−8, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).

claim: The top significant GO terms were 'embryonic digit morphogenesis' and 'embryonic appendage morphogenesis' (FDR < 1 × 10−8).
source: A gene ontology enrichment analysis for the 24 face-associated genetic loci (Table 1) highlighted a total of 67 biological process terms and seven molecular function terms significantly enriched with different genes group (FDR < 0.01 or q value < 0.01, Supplementary file 1 - Table 15), with the top significant terms being 'embryonic digit morphogenesis' and 'embryonic appendage morphogenesis' (FDR < 1 × 10−8, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Directly stated with specific FDR value.

claim: Significant multi-tissue cis-eQTL effects (adjusted p<0.05) were found around three genes, ARHGEF19, RPE65, and TBX15.
source: Significant multi-tissue cis-eQTL effects (adjusted p<0.05) were found around three genes, ARHGEF19, RPE65, and TBX15 (Supplementary file 1 - Table 16).
evidence: Directly stated with statistical threshold and reference to supplementary data.

claim: In 89% of 9 embryonic stem cells, 65% of 20 different tissue cells, and 15% of 20 primary cells, the 24 genes showed significantly higher expression in all cell types (p<0.05) after multiple testing correction compared to the background genes.
source: In 89% of 9 embryonic stem cells, 65% of 20 different tissue cells, and 15% of 20 primary cells these 24 genes showed significantly higher expression in all cell types (p<0.05) after multiple testing correction compared to the background genes (Figure 4A), and the most significant difference was observed in CNCCs (p=3.8 × 10−6).
evidence: Directly stated with percentages and statistical threshold.

claim: The most significant difference in gene expression was observed in CNCCs (p=3.8 × 10−6).
source: In 89% of 9 embryonic stem cells, 65% of 20 different tissue cells, and 15% of 20 primary cells these 24 genes showed significantly higher expression in all cell types (p<0.05) after multiple testing correction compared to the background genes (Figure 4A), and the most significant difference was observed in CNCCs (p=3.8 × 10−6).
evidence: Directly stated with specific p-value.

claim: 16 (66.7%) of the 24 genes showed preferential expression in CNCCs compared to 49 other cell types.
source: Specifically, 16 (66.7%) of these 24 genes showed preferential expression in CNCCs compared to 49 other cell types.
evidence: Directly stated with specific percentage.

claim: The top-ranked three preferentially expressed genes in CNCCs were PAX3 (p=1.3 × 10−29), INTU (p=8.3 × 10−25), and ROR2 (p=4.5 × 10−23).
source: The top-ranked three preferentially expressed genes were PAX3 (p=1.3 × 10−29), INTU (p=8.3 × 10−25), and ROR2 (p=4.5 × 10−23, Figure 4B).
evidence: Directly stated with specific p-values.

claim: 6 (25%) of the 24 face-associated loci showed significant enrichment of cis-regulatory entries at the top 0.1% of the genome level in at least one epigenomic tracks after Bonferroni correction (adjusted p<0.05).
source: In particular, 6 (25%) of the 24 face-associated loci, that is 1p36.13 ARHGEF19, 2q36.1 PAX3, CMSS1, 4q28.1 INTU, 16q12.1 SALL1, and 16q12.2 RPGRIP1L, showed significant enrichment of cis-regulatory entries at the top 0.1% of the genome level in at least one epigenomic tracks after Bonferroni correction (adjusted p<0.05, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).

claim: Luciferase reporter assays in CD271+ neural crest progenitor cells demonstrated that both SNPs in 2q36.1 and 4q28.1, respectively, showed statistically significant allele-specific effects on enhancer activity.
source: Luciferase reporter assays in CD271+ neural crest progenitor cells demonstrated that both SNPs in 2q36.1 and 4q28.1, respectively, showed statistically significant allele-specific effects on enhancer activity (Figure 5C).
evidence: Directly stated with reference to experimental results.

claim: In the 4q28.1 region, the derived SNP alleles were associated with decreased luciferase expression (33.5 ×~ 10.4 ×) as well as a reduced length of some nose features (−0.087 < beta < −0.078).
source: In the 4q28.1 region, the derived SNP alleles were associated with decreased luciferase expression (33.5 ×~ 10.4 × , Supplementary file 1 - Table 18) as well as a reduced length of some nose features (−0.087 < beta < −0.078, Supplementary file 1 - Table 7).
evidence: Directly stated with specific values and reference to supplementary data.

claim: In the 2q36.1 region, the derived SNP alleles were associated with increased luciferase expression (1.5 ×~ 3.7 ×) as well as an increased length of some nasion-related features (0.131 < beta < 0.149).
source: In the 2q36.1 region, the derived SNP alleles were associated with increased luciferase expression (1.5 ×~ 3.7 × , Supplementary file 1 - Table 18) as well as an increased length of some nasion-related features (0.131 < beta < 0.149, Supplementary file 1 - Table 7).
evidence: Directly stated with specific values and reference to supplementary data.

claim: The overlapping loci from independent facial GWASs include DNA variants in or close to 10 genes: CACNA2D3, DCHS2, EPHB3, HOXD cluster, PAX1, PAX3, PKDCC, SOX9, SUPT3H, and TBX15.
source: The overlapping loci from independent facial GWASs, thus currently representing the most established genetic findings, include DNA variants in or close to 10 genes that is CACNA2D3 (Paternoster et al., 2012; Pickrell et al., 2016), DCHS2 (Adhikari et al., 2016; Claes et al., 2018), EPHB3 (Claes et al., 2018; Pickrell et al., 2016), HOXD cluster (Claes et al., 2018; Pickrell et al., 2016), PAX1 (Adhikari et al., 2016; Shaffer et al., 2016), PAX3 (Adhikari et al., 2016; Claes et al., 2018; Liu et al., 2012; Paternoster et al., 2012; Pickrell et al., 2016), PKDCC (Claes et al., 2018; Pickrell et al., 2016), SOX9 (Cha et al., 2018; Claes et al., 2018; Pickrell et al., 2016), SUPT3H (Adhikari et al., 2016; Claes et al., 2018; Pickrell et al., 2016), and TBX15 (Claes et al., 2018; Pickrell et al., 2016), which were identified mostly in Europeans.
evidence: Directly stated with citations to previous studies.

claim: INTU, also known as planar cell polarity (PCP) effector, has been reported to compromise proteolytic processing of Gli3 by regulating Hh signal transduction.
source: INTU, also known as planar cell polarity (PCP) effector, has been reported to compromise proteolytic processing of Gli3 by regulating Hh signal transduction (Zeng et al., 2010).
evidence: Directly stated with citation to previous study.

claim: SNPs in the GLI3 region have been previously associated with human nose wing breadth.
source: Notably, SNPs in the GLI3 region have been previously associated with human nose wing breadth (Adhikari et al., 2016), supporting a link between INTU and facial morphogenesis.
evidence: Directly stated with citation to previous study.

claim: Rare frameshift mutations in INTU have been found to cause human Oral-Facial-Digital (OFD) syndromes as characterized by abnormalities of the face and oral cavity.
source: In addition, rare frameshift mutations in INTU have been found to cause human Oral-Facial-Digital (OFD) syndromes as characterized by abnormalities of the face and oral cavity (Bruel et al., 2017).
evidence: Directly stated with citation to previous study.

source: A previous study found that Rpgrip1l mutant mouse embryos displayed facial abnormalities in cleft upper lips and hypoplastic lower jaws (Delous et al., 2007).

source: FTO, a proximate gene to RPGRIP1L, has also been found essential for normal bone growth and bone mineralization in mice (Sachse et al., 2018).
evidence: Directly stated with citation to previous study.

source: TBX3, a member of the T-box gene family, causes Ulnar-mammary syndrome which is a rare disorder characterized by distinct chin and nose shape together with many other abnormal morphological changes (Bamshad et al., 1997; Joss et al., 2011).
evidence: Directly stated with citations to previous studies.

claim: The homologous Kif6 transcript sequence was necessary for spine development in zebrafish, likely due to its role in cilia, which is known to utilize neural crest cells for regulating ventral forebrain morphogenesis.
source: It has been shown that the homologous Kif6 transcript sequence was necessary for spine development in zebrafish, likely due to its role in cilia, which is known to utilize neural crest cells for regulating ventral forebrain morphogenesis (Buchan et al., 2014).

claim: A Ror2 knockout mouse has been used as a model for the developmental pathology of autosomal recessive Robinow syndrome, a human dwarfism syndrome characterized by limb shortening, vertebral and craniofacial malformations, and small external genitalia.
source: A Ror2 knockout mouse has been used as a model for the developmental pathology of autosomal recessive Robinow syndrome, a human dwarfism syndrome characterized by limb shortening, vertebral and craniofacial malformations, and small external genitalia (Schwabe et al., 2004).
evidence: Directly stated with citation to previous study.

claim: DCAF4L2 gene variants were previously associated with NSCL/P.
source: DCAF4L2 gene variants were previously associated with NSCL/P (Leslie et al., 2017; Ludwig et al., 2012; Yu et al., 2017) and we revealed a significant effect on the distance between alares and the upper-lip.

claim: Pleiotropic effects of TBX15 on skeleton, for example stature, were previously demonstrated by a large-sized GWAS.
source: Moreover, pleiotropic effects of TBX15 on skeleton, for example stature, were previously demonstrated by a large-sized GWAS (Wood et al., 2014).

source: Loss of function of TBX15 in mice has been shown to cause abnormal skeletal development (Singh et al., 2005).

source: Of the previously identified face-associated genetic loci, several candidate genes for example Pax3 (Zalc et al., 2015), Prdm16 (Bjork et al., 2010), Tp63 (Thomason et al., 2008), Sfrp2 (Satoh et al., 2008), and Gli3 (Hui and Joyner, 1993) have been shown to play important roles in cranial development of embryonic mice.
evidence: Directly stated with citations to previous studies.

claim: In adult mice only Edar has been investigated for its effect on normal facial variation.
source: Moreover, in adult mice only Edar has been investigated for its effect on normal facial variation (Adhikari et al., 2016), but the respective face-associated missense EDARV370A is nearly absent in Europeans (Kamberov et al., 2013).
evidence: Directly stated with citations to previous studies.

claim: The respective face-associated missense EDARV370A is nearly absent in Europeans.
source: Moreover, in adult mice only Edar has been investigated for its effect on normal facial variation (Adhikari et al., 2016), but the respective face-associated missense EDARV370A is nearly absent in Europeans (Kamberov et al., 2013).
evidence: Directly stated with citation to previous study.

claim: Nasal shape, which is essential for humidifying and warming the air before it reaches the sensitive lungs, has been found to significantly correlate with climatic variables such as temperature and humidity in human populations.
source: For example, nasal shape, which is essential for humidifying and warming the air before it reaches the sensitive lungs, has been found to significantly correlate with climatic variables such as temperature and humidity in human populations (Noback et al., 2011).
evidence: Directly stated with citation to previous study.

claim: EDAR clearly demonstrates an Asian specific effect, which impacts on various ectoderm-derived appearance traits such as hair morphology, size of the breast, facial shape in Asians.
source: However, there are existing examples of population-specific effects, for example, EDAR clearly demonstrates an Asian specific effect, which impacts on various ectoderm-derived appearance traits such as hair morphology, size of the breast, facial shape in Asians (Adhikari et al., 2015; Kamberov et al., 2013; Kimura et al., 2009; Tan et al., 2013).
evidence: Directly stated with citations to previous studies.

claim: The human face represents a combined set of highly heritable phenotypes.
source: The human face represents a combined set of highly heritable phenotypes, but knowledge on its genetic architecture remains limited, despite the relevance for various fields.

source: A series of genome-wide association studies on 78 facial shape phenotypes quantified from 3-dimensional facial images of 10,115 Europeans identified 24 genetic loci reaching study-wide suggestive association (p < 5 × 10−8), among which 17 were previously unreported.

claim: A follow-up multi-ethnic study in additional 7917 individuals confirmed 10 loci including six unreported ones (padjusted < 2.1 × 10−3).
source: A follow-up multi-ethnic study in additional 7917 individuals confirmed 10 loci including six unreported ones (padjusted < 2.1 × 10−3).

source: A global map of derived polygenic face scores assembled facial features in major continental groups consistent with anthropological knowledge.

source: Analyses of epigenomic datasets from cranial neural crest cells revealed abundant cis-regulatory activities at the face-associated genetic loci.

claim: Luciferase reporter assays in neural crest progenitor cells highlighted enhancer activities of several face-associated DNA variants.
source: Luciferase reporter assays in neural crest progenitor cells highlighted enhancer activities of several face-associated DNA variants.

claim: The human face represents a multi-dimensional set of correlated, mostly symmetric, complex phenotypes with high heritability.
source: The human face represents a multi-dimensional set of correlated, mostly symmetric, complex phenotypes with high heritability.
evidence: Directly stated in the introduction.

claim: There is a large degree of facial similarity between monozygotic twins and, albeit less so, between other relatives.
source: This is illustrated by a large degree of facial similarity between monozygotic twins and, albeit less so, between other relatives (Djordjevic et al., 2016), stable facial features within and differences between major human populations, and the enormous diversity among unrelated persons almost at the level of human individualization.
evidence: Directly stated with citation to previous study.

claim: Current knowledge on the specific genes influencing human facial appearance and the underlying molecular mechanisms forming facial morphology is limited.
source: However, current knowledge on the specific genes influencing human facial appearance and the underlying molecular mechanisms forming facial morphology is limited.
evidence: Directly stated in the introduction.

claim: Nine separate genome-wide association studies (GWASs) have each highlighted several but largely non-overlapping genetic loci associated with facial shape phenotypes.
source: Over recent years, nine separate genome-wide association studies (GWASs) have each highlighted several but largely non-overlapping genetic loci associated with facial shape phenotypes (Adhikari et al., 2016; Cha et al., 2018; Claes et al., 2018; Cole et al., 2016; Lee et al., 2017; Liu et al., 2012; Paternoster et al., 2012; Pickrell et al., 2016; Shaffer et al., 2016).
evidence: Directly stated with citations to previous studies.

claim: The true number of genes that influence polygenetic facial traits is likely to be much larger than currently known.
source: Indicated by the small effect size of the previously identified face-associated DNA variants, together with the high heritability of facial phenotypes, the true number of genes that influence polygenetic facial traits is likely to be much larger than currently known.
evidence: Inference based on small effect sizes and high heritability.

claim: Our understanding of the complex genetic architecture of human facial morphology remains largely incomplete.
source: Despite the previous work, our understanding of the complex genetic architecture of human facial morphology thus remains largely incomplete.
evidence: Directly stated in the introduction.

claim: Variants at genetic loci implicated in human facial shape are involved in the epigenetic regulation of human neural crest cells.
source: A most recent study (Claes et al., 2018) suggested that variants at genetic loci implicated in human facial shape are involved in the epigenetic regulation of human neural crest cells, suggesting that at least some of the functional variants may reside within regulatory elements such as enhancers.
evidence: Directly stated with citation to previous study.

claim: Experimental studies have proven enhancer effects of pigmentation-associated DNA variants.
source: Although this is in line with evidence for other appearance phenotypes such as human pigmentation traits, where experimental studies have proven enhancer effects of pigmentation-associated DNA variants (Visser et al., 2012; Visser et al., 2014; Visser et al., 2015), experimental evidence for understanding the functional basis of DNA variants for which facial phenotype associations have been previously established is missing as of yet.
evidence: Directly stated with citations to previous studies.

claim: Experimental evidence for understanding the functional basis of DNA variants for which facial phenotype associations have been previously established is missing as of yet.
source: Although this is in line with evidence for other appearance phenotypes such as human pigmentation traits, where experimental studies have proven enhancer effects of pigmentation-associated DNA variants (Visser et al., 2012; Visser et al., 2014; Visser et al., 2015), experimental evidence for understanding the functional basis of DNA variants for which facial phenotype associations have been previously established is missing as of yet.
evidence: Directly stated in the introduction.

claim: Embryonic cranial neural crest cells (CNCCs) arise during weeks 3–6 of human gestation from the dorsal part of the neural tube ectoderm and migrate into the branchial arches.
source: Embryonic cranial neural crest cells (CNCCs) arise during weeks 3–6 of human gestation from the dorsal part of the neural tube ectoderm and migrate into the branchial arches. They later form the embryonic face, consequently establishing the central plan of facial morphology and determining species-specific and individual facial variation (Bronner and LeDouarin, 2012; Cordero et al., 2011).
evidence: Directly stated with citations to previous studies.

claim: CNCCs later form the embryonic face, consequently establishing the central plan of facial morphology and determining species-specific and individual facial variation.
source: Embryonic cranial neural crest cells (CNCCs) arise during weeks 3–6 of human gestation from the dorsal part of the neural tube ectoderm and migrate into the branchial arches. They later form the embryonic face, consequently establishing the central plan of facial morphology and determining species-specific and individual facial variation (Bronner and LeDouarin, 2012; Cordero et al., 2011).
evidence: Directly stated with citations to previous studies.

claim: CNCCs have been successfully derived in-vitro from human embryonic stem cells or induced pluripotent stem cells.
source: Recently, CNCCs have been successfully derived in-vitro from human embryonic stem cells or induced pluripotent stem cells (Prescott et al., 2015).

source: Out of those, a total of 44 (36%) SNPs showed significant association on either the same set of facial phenotypes or at least one facial phenotypes in a combined test, after Bonferroni correction for the number of SNPs (adjusted p<0.05) (Supplementary file 1 - Table 8).
